title: Communicating With Those We Like and Care About After Termination
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece addresses the awkward aftermath of letting go a well-liked colleague who has simply outgrown fit with the organization. The author's central claim is that most leaders let contact quietly lapse after a departure because re-engaging feels uncomfortable, and that this silence compounds over time until the relationship dissolves entirely. The recommended practice is to push through the discomfort and maintain a steady cadence of contact immediately after the departure, treating that discipline as proof the relationship, not just the job, was genuinely valued.
points: Leaders often let contact with a departed, well-liked colleague quietly lapse because reaching out feels awkward, which lets the relationship dissolve.
The discomfort of a termination is often smaller than the ongoing discomfort of avoiding contact afterward, but leaders default to avoidance anyway.
Maintaining a steady cadence of contact immediately after a departure is what actually proves the relationship was valued, not just the working arrangement.
True leaders never delegate the difficult conversations leading up to a colleague's departure to someone else.
quotes: But sometimes the organization outgrows a valued colleague when their skills and talents no longer match what the enterprise needs now.
True leaders never delegate the tough conversations leading up to the colleague’s departure.
Unfortunately, once interaction ceases to exist for a few weeks, reengaging becomes even harder.
The real challenge is to maintain a steady cadence of contact immediately after the dismissal, no matter how difficult or awkward it may be.
If this person was truly valued and prized, then leaders really have no other choice. That’s what authenticity is all about.
